reviews.review:
(Full disclosure: I know the creator of this game and have briefly tested pre-release versions)

Minerva Labyrinth is best described imo as an indie interpretation of Operation Abyss combined with a healthy dose of western DRPG design sensibilities. For example, dungeons themselves are brutal and have thoughtful puzzles, and all skills and abilities have detailed minutae and often secondary effects. 

[Note: Every line of code*, every pixel of visuals, and every note of music was created by one person. No commissions or assets were purchased, no outside help was given, and absolutely no AI was ever used even once. If this intrigues you, read on.]

*outside of the Godot engine core ;) 

The game begins with having you create a party of 5 by choosing a primary “aspect”, or class, a secondary which determines a powerful passive, and stats, which determine what equipment you can wield. The aspects themselves are fairly varied; even classes which share healing abilities tend to play quite differently (for instance, Love is a more reactionary healing class, while Sun is an active one). 
You will find you will mesh better with some aspects than others. I tend to enjoy Water and Hunt for their combat flow affecting abilities, but others may prefer War and Destruction for pure damage output. You can’t respec, so you might even want to start a couple new games to try out all the basic abilities to get a feel for everyone.

(If you wish you can skip the tutorial level and you will be placed at HQ at level 2.)

The general game loop is: Go to dungeon, explore as far as you can or until you kill the big baddie, retreat and rest. Each “area” has 3-4 floors or sub-areas each, making them a decent size, and they house the occasional secret and at least one major thinky-based puzzle. 

Exploration is generally rewarded with unique pieces of equipment that can usually fill power gaps that may exist in your party. 

Combat can be quite tough, especially at first before you are accustomed to your class skills and before more options and spells open up. Save in dungeons frequently and retreat when you must - but not too often, else you’ll find yourself out of money from resting too much. Bosses will always test your party makeup and endurance and often have you breathing a sigh when they finally fall.

The bottom line is, if you’re looking for a DRPG, this will scratch the itch. If it looks like you’ll enjoy it, you’ll enjoy it. It’s been thoughtfully put together from absolute scratch and the care is tangible. 

There are no bugs or crashes. It plays well with gamepad, keyboard, mouse, or kb+m with fully customizable controls. The interface is easy to read, and even supports colorblind options. 

Expect about 20 hours, 15 if you’re a good crawler. Worth the admission.
